title: ICMR Study Links Vitamin D and B12 Deficiencies to Higher Dementia Risk in Indian Adults
excerpt: A landmark study of 570 adults in Telangana found that nearly 40% had elevated dementia risk, with deficiencies in vitamins D, B2, B6, and B12 significantly more common among those at higher risk.
body:
• Nearly 40% of study participants were classified as having higher predicted dementia risk, with vitamin deficiencies significantly more prevalent in this group
  • Deficiencies in vitamins D, B2, B6, and B12 were markedly more common among those with elevated risk scores
  • Rural participants showed higher vulnerability than urban counterparts, highlighting geographic disparities in nutrition
  • The study, published in The Lancet Regional Health, was conducted in collaboration with Stanford and the Karolinska Institute

A study by the Indian Council of Medical Research-National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN) in Hyderabad has established a clear link between micronutrient deficiencies and elevated dementia risk among Indian adults, pointing to nutrition as a critical and modifiable factor in brain health.

The community-based cross-sectional research, published in The Lancet Regional Health – Southeast Asia in June 2026, examined 570 middle-aged and older adults between 40 and 80 years from both rural and urban areas of Telangana. Researchers used a culturally adapted version of the Cardiovascular Risk Factors, Ageing and Incidence of Dementia (CAIDE) score to assess dementia risk, alongside the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) tool for cognitive evaluation.

Key Findings: Widespread Deficiencies Among At-Risk Group

The results were striking. Approximately 40% of participants were classified as being in the higher-risk category for cognitive decline. Those in this group consistently showed poorer nutritional status compared with lower-risk participants.

Deficiencies of vitamins D, B2 (riboflavin), B6, and B12 were markedly more prevalent among participants with higher dementia risk scores. The at-risk group also reported lower dietary diversity, consumed more saturated fats, and had lower intake of unsaturated fats — a pattern that researchers said pointed to systemic nutritional gaps.

Diets rich in micronutrients, particularly fruits and vegetables, were associated with a lower dementia risk-factor burden, according to the study, suggesting that dietary improvements could serve as a practical intervention.

Rural-Urban Divide in Nutritional Health

A notable divide emerged between rural and urban participants. Vitamin deficiencies were significantly more common among rural residents, indicating region-specific vulnerabilities that may compound existing healthcare gaps in India's countryside.

Despite higher levels of physical activity among rural populations, their nutritional deficits contributed to an elevated dementia risk profile — a finding that researchers said underscored the need for targeted public health interventions in underserved areas.

"As India's ageing population continues to expand, the number of people living with dementia is expected to rise substantially by 2050. Our findings highlight that micronutrient status is closely linked with the burden of dementia risk factors among Indian adults."

— Dr G Bhanuprakash Reddy, Lead Investigator, ICMR-NIN

Implications for India's Aging Population

The findings arrive at a critical moment. India is witnessing a rapid increase in its elderly population due to rising life expectancy, and low- and middle-income countries, including India, account for nearly 60% of the global dementia burden. While genetic factors play a role, researchers noted that nearly half of dementia cases are linked to modifiable risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity, smoking, depression, and social isolation.

Dr Bharati Kulkarni, Director of ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition, emphasized the preventive angle. "Given that effective disease-modifying therapies for dementia remain limited, prevention through early identification of risk factors and timely intervention becomes increasingly important," she said, according to Hyderabad Mail. "This study provides important evidence that nutritional factors, especially micronutrient status, should be integrated into dementia prevention strategies in future."

The study was conducted in collaboration with researchers from the Stanford Center for Innovation in Global Health in the United States and the Karolinska Institute in Sweden, lending international credibility to the findings.

What This Means for the Indian Diaspora

For NRIs with aging parents in India, the study highlights a practical concern: ensuring elderly family members maintain adequate vitamin intake and dietary diversity. Vitamin B12 deficiency is particularly common among older vegetarians — a significant demographic in India — while vitamin D deficiency remains widespread despite the country's tropical climate, often due to limited sun exposure among the elderly.

Dr Reddy cautioned that while the cross-sectional design restricts the ability to draw causal inferences, the study makes a strong case that "nutrition, particularly micronutrient adequacy and dietary diversity, represents a modifiable factor that can be targeted through public health interventions."
